title: Origins and History
description: Signature soccer begins with a folk game made fair by a rulebook: England's 1863 Laws turned village ball games into a sport strangers could play together. The spread that followed was not imposed from above but carried by ordinary people, sailors and teachers and workers, who took a ball and a set of rules wherever they went. The 1930 World Cup in Uruguay gave that worldwide game a championship, and the game's simplicity has kept it open ever since: a ball, two goals, and eleven per side are enough to start. That openness is soccer's strength, because the same laws govern a schoolyard match and a World Cup final.

demo.code:
print('Codification:', 1863)
print('First World Cup: Uruguay 1930')
print('Gap:', 1930-1863, 'years')
demo.expected_output:
Codification: 1863
First World Cup: Uruguay 1930
Gap: 67 years

history: Modern soccer was codified in England in 1863 with the Laws of the Game, and the first World Cup was held in Uruguay in 1930.
competitions: The World Cup, continental championships, and club competitions now draw the largest audiences in world sport.
rules: The Laws of the Game, maintained by the International Football Association Board, govern soccer worldwide.

title: Laws of the Game
description: Signature soccer law is seventeen rules that fit on a few pages yet govern the world's biggest game. The essentials are easy to state: ninety minutes, eleven per side, a goal only when the whole ball crosses the line, and no deliberate handball except by the goalkeeper in the penalty area. Offside is the law that shapes tactics most, because it stops attackers from camping by the goal and forces teams to time their runs. Cards give the referee a graduated response, a caution in yellow and a sending-off in red, and restarts, from throw-ins to penalty kicks, keep the game flowing after every stoppage. Simplicity at the top, depth underneath: that is why the Laws have lasted.

print('Laws of the Game:', 17)
print('Halves: 2 x 45 =', 2*45, 'minutes')
print('Cards: yellow caution, red sending-off')
demo.expected_output:
Laws of the Game: 17
Halves: 2 x 45 = 90 minutes
Cards: yellow caution, red sending-off

rules: A match lasts 90 minutes in two 45-minute halves, with 11 players per side, one goalkeeper, and goals scored when the whole ball crosses the goal line.
history: The Laws are maintained by the International Football Association Board, with FIFA publishing them for worldwide use.
techniques: Referees enforce fouls, offside, handball, and misconduct, using yellow and red cards and, in some competitions, video review.

title: Positions and Formations
description: Signature positions are a division of labour: the goalkeeper guards, defenders stop, midfielders link, and forwards finish. A formation name like 4-4-2 or 4-3-3 is shorthand for that division, counting defenders, midfielders, and forwards in order, and it tells a viewer where a team's strength lies. The numbers are not cages, though: a fullback may attack like a winger, a midfielder may drop into defence, and a team may defend in one shape and attack in another. Coaches change shape mid-match to chase a goal or protect a lead, and players who understand their role and their neighbours' roles are the ones who make those changes work.
techniques: Goalkeeper, defenders, midfielders, and forwards each have distinct duties, and formations such as 4-4-2 and 4-3-3 describe their arrangement.
rules: Teams may use substitutes within competition limits, and formations may change during a match as coaches adjust tactics.
training: Players train for their position's demands: defenders for tackling and heading, midfielders for passing and stamina, forwards for finishing.

title: Passing and Possession
description: Signature passing is a conversation between feet: a pass asks a teammate to move, and the teammate's run answers it. First touch decides the conversation's quality, because a heavy touch kills a move and a soft touch keeps it alive. Weight matters as much as direction: a ball played too hard runs past its target, a ball played too softly is intercepted, and the right weight lets a runner meet it at full speed. Possession is the strategy built on those passes: keep the ball, move the defence, tire the opponent, and wait for a gap. But possession without penetration is sterile, and the best teams know when to stop passing sideways and play the ball that splits a line.

demo.code:
attempted = 400
complete = 340
print('Attempted:', attempted)
print('Completed:', complete)
print('Rate:', round(complete / attempted * 100, 1), '%')

techniques: Short passes, long passes, one-touch passing, and through balls move the ball and the defence, with first touch and weight of pass as core skills.
training: Passing drills build accuracy, timing, and movement off the ball, since a pass is only as good as the run that receives it.
statistics: Possession and pass completion are tracked as team statistics, though they measure control, not necessarily goals.

title: Shooting and Finishing
description: Signature finishing is decision-making under pressure: power or placement, early shot or extra touch, near post or far post. The instep drives, the inside of the foot places, the volley meets a ball in the air, and the header turns a cross into a goal, but the technique matters less than the choice. A calm finisher picks a corner before shooting and commits to it, while a hurried finisher snatches at the ball and gives the goalkeeper a chance. Distance flatters the shooter and favours the keeper, so coaches preach the unglamorous truth: the best chance is usually the closest one, taken quickly, with the foot that gives control rather than the foot that gives spectacle.

demo.code:
shots = 10
on_target = 4
goals = 1
print('Shots:', shots, 'On target:', on_target, 'Goals:', goals)
print('Conversion:', round(goals / shots * 100, 1), '%')

techniques: Shooting uses the instep for power, the inside of the foot for placement, volleys, headers, and chips, with composure deciding many chances.
training: Finishing drills practise shooting from different angles, distances, and speeds, under pressure from defenders and the goalkeeper.
rules: A goal counts when the whole ball crosses the goal line, and shots from inside the penalty area are more likely to score than long-range efforts.

title: Defending and Tackling
description: Signature defending starts with a simple rule: stay between your attacker and your goal. From there it becomes a team art, because a back line that steps up together can catch attackers offside, while a line that steps up in pieces invites a through ball. Jockeying, delaying an attacker without diving in, buys time for teammates to recover, and a clean tackle is one that wins the ball without endangering the opponent. Reckless tackles cost more than a free kick: they cost cards, suspensions, and the trust of a defence that must hold together. The best defenders are rarely the most spectacular; they are the ones whose opponents never get a clean chance.

demo.code:
attempts = 15
success = 11
print('Tackles:', attempts, 'Won:', success)
print('Rate:', round(success / attempts * 100, 1), '%')

techniques: Defenders jockey attackers, stay goal-side, tackle cleanly, block shots, and head clearances, with teamwork in pressing and covering.
rules: Tackles must win the ball without endangering opponents; reckless or excessive force is a foul and may bring a card.
training: Defensive drills practise one-on-one defending, tracking runners, and organising a back line that moves as a unit.

title: Goalkeeping
description: Signature goalkeeping is a position apart: the only hands allowed on the field, and only inside the penalty area. The goalkeeper's first skill is not diving but positioning, because standing at the right angle makes the goal smaller before a shot is even taken. Handling choices follow from the ball: catch what can be held, parry what cannot, punch what is too dangerous to catch, and claim crosses before attackers reach them. Distribution is the modern goalkeeper's second job, with throws, kicks, and passes that start attacks instead of merely ending them. It is a lonely role, where one mistake is a goal, but it is also the role that can win a match with a single save.

demo.code:
faced = 10
stopped = 7
print('Faced:', faced, 'Saved:', stopped)
print('Save rate:', round(stopped / faced * 100, 1), '%')

techniques: Goalkeepers dive, catch, parry, and punch, position themselves by angles, and distribute with throws, kicks, and passes.
rules: Only the goalkeeper may handle the ball, and only inside the penalty area; outside it, the goalkeeper is an outfield player.
training: Goalkeeper training covers footwork, handling, diving technique, crosses, one-on-ones, and communication with defenders.

title: Set Pieces
description: Signature set pieces are the game's planned plays: moments when the ball is dead and a team can execute something it rehearsed all week. The penalty, twelve yards and only the goalkeeper to beat, is the purest scoring chance soccer offers, which is why penalty takers practise placement under pressure. Corners turn the penalty area into a crowded contest of runs, blocks, and headers, with defenders choosing between marking a man and guarding a zone. Free kicks offer a choice, shoot or cross, and throw-ins, the humblest restart, can catch a defence napping when taken fast. Tight matches are often decided here, not by open play brilliance but by a routine executed cleanly.

demo.code:
taken = 5
made = 4
print('Penalties:', taken, 'Scored:', made)
print('Rate:', round(made / taken * 100, 1), '%')

techniques: Free kicks, corners, penalties, and throw-ins are rehearsed plays, with deliveries, runs, blocks, and shots planned in training.
rules: A penalty kick is taken from 12 yards with only the goalkeeper to beat; corners are taken from the corner arc; free kicks may be direct or indirect.
training: Teams practise set-piece routines for attacking and defending, since a large share of goals in tight matches come from them.

title: Tactics and Systems
description: Signature tactics are shared plans for the moments between attack and defence. Pressing hunts the ball high, counterattacking defends deep and breaks fast, possession probes patiently, and a low block defends compactly and frustrates. Each system has a price: pressing tires a team, counterattacking concedes territory, possession risks sterile passing, and a low block invites pressure. A coach's job is to match the system to the players available and to the opponent's weakness, and then to change it mid-match when the plan stops working. Players make tactics real by moving together, because a pressing forward without pressing midfielders is just a tired forward.

print('Each system has a cost; coaches match system to players')
demo.expected_output:
Press: win high. Counter: break fast. Possess: probe. Low block: frustrate.
Each system has a cost; coaches match system to players

techniques: Pressing, counterattacking, possession play, and low blocks are tactical systems, chosen to suit a team's players and opponents.
history: Tactical ideas have evolved from early attacking formations to modern pressing and positional play, shaped by influential coaches and teams.
training: Tactical training uses small-sided games, video analysis, and match scenarios to teach players when to press, drop, or switch play.

title: Training and Fitness
description: Signature soccer fitness is built for a game that never lets a player rest for long: repeated sprints, sharp turns, and skills performed while tired. Training therefore mixes technique with conditioning, because a pass practised fresh is not the same as a pass made in the eightieth minute. Small-sided games are the coach's best tool, since they combine fitness, tactics, and ball touches in one exercise, while strength work protects hamstrings, groins, and ankles, the injuries that most often interrupt a season. Load is planned like a budget: too much spending causes injury, too little leaves a team unfit, and the balance shifts across a season toward freshness before big matches.

training: Soccer training mixes technical drills, small-sided games, strength and conditioning, and recovery, planned across a season.
safety: Warm-ups, load management, and injury prevention exercises reduce the risk of muscle injuries, the most common soccer injuries.
techniques: Fitness demands include repeated sprints, endurance, agility, and jumping, with position-specific demands for each role.

title: Youth Development
description: Signature youth soccer succeeds when it gives children the ball, not a lecture: small pitches, small goals, and small-sided games mean many touches and constant decisions. De-emphasising league tables at young ages is a deliberate choice, because a child who fears a table will play safe, while a child who enjoys the game will try, fail, and improve. Academies add structure for talented players, with coaching, schooling, and welfare, but they serve a minority, and the majority's prize is different: a lifelong love of playing. Coaches who protect that love, with qualified training and safeguarding, do more for soccer than any single trophy a youth team might win.

print('Small pitches and goals suit young players')
demo.expected_output:
Session: 60 minutes for 10 children
Small pitches and goals suit young players

training: Youth soccer emphasises small-sided games, many touches, and fun, with formal league tables and results de-emphasised at younger ages.
safety: Age-group rules, qualified coaches, safeguarding, and appropriate pitch and goal sizes protect young players.
history: Academies run by professional clubs scout and develop young talent, with education and welfare as formal parts of academy life.

title: Refereeing
description: Signature refereeing is judgement at sprint speed: the referee must see, decide, and signal while twenty-two players and a crowd press for the opposite call. Assistants judge offside and touchline incidents, the fourth official manages benches and substitutions, and video review, where used, checks only clear errors in goals, penalties, red cards, and mistaken identity. Fitness is a referee's hidden qualification, because a referee who cannot keep up cannot be in position to see. The culture around refereeing matters too: players who accept decisions, even ones they dispute, keep the match playable, and abuse of officials drives good referees away from the game.

print('Referee plus two assistants plus fourth official')
print('Video review covers clear errors only, in some competitions')
demo.expected_output:
Referee plus two assistants plus fourth official
Video review covers clear errors only, in some competitions

rules: The referee controls the match, applies the Laws, keeps time, and is assisted by assistant referees, a fourth official, and video review in some competitions.
techniques: Referees train in positioning, fitness, communication, and decision-making, and are assessed after matches.
history: Refereeing developed with codified soccer, and video assistant refereeing was introduced in major competitions in the late 2010s.

title: Major Competitions
description: Signature competitions are the calendar of soccer: leagues that reward consistency across a season, and cups that reward nerve in a single match. The World Cup, every four years since 1930, is the national game's summit, while continental championships and the Champions League give clubs and regions their own summits. Promotion and relegation tie domestic divisions together, so a small club can climb and a large club can fall, which keeps leagues honest. Tournament formats blend fairness and drama: group stages give every team several matches, knockout rounds give every match finality, and extra time and penalties decide ties that neither team could break in open play.

competitions: The World Cup, continental championships, and club competitions such as the UEFA Champions League are soccer's premier tournaments.
history: The World Cup began in 1930, the European Championship in 1960, and continental club competitions grew through the twentieth century.
rules: Tournaments use group stages followed by knockout rounds, with extra time and penalty shootouts deciding tied knockout matches.

title: Women's Football
description: Signature women's football is a story of a ban outlasted: England's 1921 to 1971 ban, and restrictions elsewhere, did not end the women's game, because women kept playing, organising, and drawing crowds. The Women's World Cup, begun in 1991, gave that persistence a global stage, and professional leagues followed, with full-time players, growing crowds, and broadcasts that reach new audiences. The game itself needs no separate description: same Laws, same positions, same tactics, same drama. What remains is the ordinary work of equality, pay, facilities, and coverage brought up to the standard the women's game has already earned on the field.

print('Today: professional leagues and growing crowds')
demo.expected_output:
First Women's World Cup: 1991
FA ban lasted: 50 years
Today: professional leagues and growing crowds

history: Women's soccer was long restricted, including a ban by England's Football Association from 1921 to 1971, before growing into professional leagues and major tournaments.
competitions: The Women's World Cup, begun in 1991, and professional women's leagues now draw large crowds and broadcasts.
statistics: Participation and audiences for women's soccer have grown sharply, though pay and coverage gaps remain in many countries.

title: Futsal
description: Signature futsal is soccer compressed: five per side, a hard court, a low-bounce ball, and a clock that stops, so every second counts. Born in Uruguay in the 1930s for small spaces, it turns tightness into a teacher: there is no room to hide, no time to dwell, and every touch must be clean. Rolling substitutions keep the tempo high, and the flying goalkeeper, joining attacks as an extra player, adds a tactical gamble unique to the indoor game. Many of soccer's finest players learned their first touch in futsal, because a small court punishes a heavy touch instantly and rewards a soft one just as fast.

print('Match: 2 x 20 stopped-clock minutes')
print('Ball: smaller, lower bounce')
demo.expected_output:
Team size: 5
Match: 2 x 20 stopped-clock minutes
Ball: smaller, lower bounce

history: Futsal was developed in Uruguay in the 1930s as indoor soccer for small spaces and is now governed by FIFA with a World Cup.
rules: Two teams of five play on a hard indoor court with a smaller, lower-bounce ball, in two 20-minute halves of stopped-clock time.
techniques: Close control, quick passing, and rapid transitions dominate, with rolling substitutions and a goalkeeper who often joins attacks.

title: Beach Soccer
description: Signature beach soccer is soccer on sand, and the sand changes everything: running costs more energy, the ball bounces less predictably, and balance becomes a skill in itself. Five per side, three periods of twelve minutes, and rolling substitutions keep the tempo high, while barefoot play and acrobatic bicycle kicks give the game its spectacle. Goals come often, because the soft surface punishes defensive mistakes and rewards bold shooting, and free kicks are a major weapon on a small pitch. Born from informal beach games, notably in Brazil, it is now a World Cup sport, proof that a game played for fun on a beach can become a contest the world takes seriously.

print('Played barefoot; goals are frequent')

history: Beach soccer grew from informal beach games, notably in Brazil, into an organised sport with a FIFA Beach Soccer World Cup.
rules: Two teams of five play on sand in three 12-minute periods, with free kicks, bicycle kicks, and a fast, high-scoring game.
techniques: Playing on sand demands balance, acrobatic shooting, and powerful volleys, with substitutions rolling freely.
